title: Tyler Perry's Madea Goes to Jail
full_review:
Those who go to the intermittently amusing sequel "Tyler Perry's Madea Goes to Jail" (Lionsgate) in search of an escapist romp may be surprised to find the outsized antics of the comically wayward, pistol-packing grandmother (Tyler Perry in drag) interspersed through a sober drama about prostitution, official corruption and class tensions within the African-American community.

Madea's latest characteristic misdeeds – driving on a long suspended license, she leads the police on a high-speed freeway chase – land her briefly in court, a turn of events that serves to introduce ambitious Atlanta, Ga. Assistant District Attorney Linda (Ion Overman), who's given charge of the case. But Madea soon beats the rap when it's revealed that the arresting officers failed to inform her of her rights.

In the same courtroom, Linda's fellow assistant district attorney and fiance Joshua (Derek Luke) has to recuse himself from a streetwalking prosecution when he discovers that the defendant, Candace (Keshia Knight Pulliam), is a childhood friend.

Despite drug-addicted Candace's initial reluctance to be redeemed, and despite pampered Linda's snobbish objections to his getting involved, Joshua – whose past with Candace includes a dark secret – perseveres in his effort to get her off the street.

He's aided by dedicated minister Ellen (Viola Davis from "Doubt") whose regular beat includes not only the city's red light district, but a nearby prison as well. It's there that the two storylines reconnect as Madea – after further comic criminality resulting from her quest for revenge after losing a parking space to another driver – and Candace are thrown into the slammer at the same time. The latter receives an inexplicably long sentence that suggests to the viewer, if not to Candace, some form of behind-the-scenes malfeasance.

Tyler, who also wrote, directed, and plays Uncle Joe and Brian, lacks a subtle touch and indulges in a few mild impieties. There's also a problem of wildly shifting tone, as scenes of tearful emotion or grim violence – Candace has an encounter with an abusive pimp – give way to puns, malapropisms and Medea's slapstick battles with the hapless law enforcement officers she refers to as "the Po Po."

And viewers of a certain age may be taken aback at the sight of "The Cosby Show's" Rudy Huxtable getting in cars with strange men and shivering through withdrawal.

Still, the dramatic parts of the movie do pay tribute to the redeeming effects of faith and forgiveness, and Ellen is a model of upright Christian service.

The film contains a prostitution theme, offscreen rape, a scene of physical abuse, drug use, some sexual and slightly irreverent humor, a few crass words and at least one use of profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
